L-account-biased.statement: The authors' account is skewed toward the meetings and conversations they took part in.

L-adt-extended.statement: Algebraic data types were extended with newtypes, strictness annotations, and named fields.

L-adt-fundamental.statement: Data types and pattern matching are fundamental to most modern functional languages, Scheme excepted.

L-adt-via-modules.statement: Haskell uses the module system, not a special abstype construct, for abstract data types, trading extra clutter for inferable operation types and a distinct type-class instance.

L-aetion-static-types.statement: Aetion chose Haskell for its rich static type system, open-source compilers and active research community, static typing catching many errors that would otherwise surface in the field.

L-algebraic-types-easy.statement: Basic algebraic types were straightforward, but pattern matching, abstract types, tuples, newtypes, records, n+k patterns and views raised issues.

L-algebraic-types-origin.statement: Algebraic data types originated in Burstall's NPL and Hope and reached ML's and Miranda's successors.

L-algorithmic-debugging.statement: In algorithmic debugging the debugger takes the initiative, descending through calls to locate the bug.

L-application-juxtaposition.statement: Function application is juxtaposition, associating to the left.

L-array-inplace-messier.statement: Array processing and algorithms relying on in-place update are messier in Haskell than in imperative languages.

L-arrows.statement: Arrows, proposed by Hughes, are an abstract view of computation like monads but more general, easier to use with syntactic support.

L-at-patterns-tight.statement: @-patterns bind more tightly than anything, breaking the simple binding rule, probably a mistake.

L-avoid-semicolon.statement: Without side effects there is no sequencing, so the committee avoided the semicolon and its imperative baggage.

L-backquote-infix.statement: A function identifier in backquotes is used infix, for generality and readability.

L-backus-lecture.statement: Backus's Turing Award lecture recast functional programming as a radical attack on the whole programming enterprise.

L-bind-vs-ml.statement: Bind is analogous to let in ML but the types record the effect, and monads give freedom in defining return and bind where ML fixes one notion of computation.

L-blessed-addenda.statement: The FFI effort spawned "Blessed Addenda", well-specified appendices to the Haskell 98 Report giving precise advice on implementing language extensions.

L-bluespec-two-level.statement: Bluespec is a two-level language: the full power of Haskell is available at compile time but almost all Haskell constructs are eliminated by a partial evaluator.

L-bottom-every-type.statement: A diverging or error expression has the value bottom, which belongs to every type.

L-bottom-tuple-distinct.statement: Whether bottom and (bottom, bottom) are distinct depends on lifted versus unlifted tuple semantics.

L-bytestring-fusion.statement: Data.ByteString represents strings as byte vectors and uses GHC's rewrite rules to program the optimiser so loop fusion happens when bytestring functions compose, the rules' correctness tested by QuickCheck.

L-cabal-hackage.statement: Cabal, led by Isaac Jones from 2004, supports constructing and distributing Haskell packages, and Hackage is a Cabal package server for finding and downloading them.

L-cbv-recursive-combinators.statement: Call-by-value languages disallow recursive combinator definitions, forcing eta-expansion that clutters code and wrecks the abstraction.

L-class-bounded-quantification.statement: A type-class constraint expresses a form of bounded quantification: a function is typed for any type that is an instance of a given class.

L-class-irritations.statement: The class system causes minor irritations, sometimes producing puzzling error messages.

L-classes-monads-symbiosis.statement: Type classes and monads had a symbiotic relationship: classes made monads accessible and popular while monadic I/O ensured the adoption of higher-kinded polymorphism.

L-clean-gui.statement: Clean's graphical I/O library was integral from early on, letting the user specify the interface with call-back data, unlike Haskell's fragmented GUI approach.

L-combinator-definition.statement: A combinator library, loosely defined, offers functions that combine functions into bigger functions.

L-combinator-dsel-same.statement: A combinator library can be seen as a domain-specific language, with little conceptual difference, the term chosen for historical reasons.

L-combinator-influential.statement: Combinator libraries embody nothing fundamentally new yet the idea has been extremely influential.

L-committee-design.statement: Haskell was to be designed by a committee, not an individual.

L-common-libraries.statement: Driven by user desire for cross-implementation compatibility, the Hugs, GHC and nhc teams began in 2001 to build a common open-source library set shipped with each compiler.

L-community-success.statement: The Haskell community's size and quality is both the indicator of its success and its cause.

L-concurrent-haskell.statement: Concurrent Haskell extends the IO monad with lightweight threads communicating through synchronised mutable MVars, inspired by Id's M-structures.

L-cons-not-evaluate.statement: Friedman and Wise framed lazy evaluation from Lisp with the slogan that cons should not evaluate its arguments.

L-conservative-language.statement: The committee intended a conservative language embodying current consensus rather than breaking new ground.

L-constructors-capitalised.statement: Data constructors are capitalised and variables are not (from Miranda), a rule extended to infix constructors, type constructors and type variables.

L-constructors-pattern-expr.statement: Data constructors serve both in pattern matching and in expressions.

L-continuation-io.statement: In the continuation I/O model each request/response pair is a transaction, a function taking failure and success continuations, and most programmers preferred it for its localised control flow.

L-core-lint.statement: A Core Lint typechecker checks each pass stays well-typed, a surprisingly strong consistency check that catches most optimiser bugs cheaply, one of the biggest benefits of a typed intermediate language.

L-core-pipeline.statement: After type checking the program is desugared into the explicitly typed Core language and processed by a long sequence of Core-to-Core optimising transformations.

L-core-systemf.statement: GHC's Core intermediate language was rebased in 1992 on Girard's System F omega plus data types, let and case, apparently the first compiler to use System F as a typed intermediate language.

L-cost-centres.statement: Sansom and Peyton Jones labelled source with cost centres to aggregate a logical task's costs, raising subtle questions that drove a formal cost semantics.

L-cost-higherorder.statement: Assigning costs to functions works poorly for higher-order functions such as map.

L-curried-uncurried.statement: Haskell supports both curried and uncurried definitions.

L-currying-history.statement: Following Frege, Schönfinkel and Curry, a two-argument function is a one-argument function returning a function, often more compact.

L-debt-to-miranda.statement: Haskell owes a considerable debt to Miranda in general inspiration and specific elements.

L-defaulting-rule.statement: An ad hoc defaulting rule picks a default type for ambiguous numeric constraints, clumsy but conservative, and relaxed further in GHCi.

L-design-slow.statement: Language design is a slow process.

L-dictionary-passing.statement: Type classes translate into dictionary-passing style by a type-directed transformation, with Gofer using a variant that minimises run-time dictionary construction.

L-distribution-maturity.statement: It took more than fifteen years for Haskell to gain enough momentum for distribution and discovery mechanisms to become important.

L-do-notation.statement: Do-notation, not monads themselves, made Haskell programs look conventionally imperative and blurred the line between pure and imperative code.

L-dozen-languages.statement: By 1987 more than a dozen non-strict purely functional languages existed, all alike in power and semantics.

L-dsel-definition.statement: A DSEL turns Haskell into a domain-specific embedded language sharing its syntax, types and modules, a term coined by Hudak.

L-dsel-host.statement: Several features make Haskell a friendly host for a DSEL: type classes, higher-order functions, infix syntax, overloaded literals, monads and arrows, and laziness.

L-dsel-structure.statement: A DSEL typically defines a data type conceptually a function, with operators combining pieces, executed by decomposing and applying them.

L-dsl-nonembedded.statement: A non-embedded DSL can use a conventional parser and interpreter, which Haskell suits too, though it excels at embedded DSLs.

L-dynamic-semantics-overloading.statement: Unlike most statically typed languages, Haskell's dynamic semantics depends on how the type checker resolves type-class overloading, making execution harder to reason about.

L-eager-evaluation.statement: Eager Haskell and optimistic evaluation explored evaluating Haskell eagerly on a uniprocessor while keeping non-strict semantics.

L-early-impractical.statement: In the early 1980s purely functional languages, though radical and elegant, were impractical: slow, memory-hungry, and lacking input/output.

L-edison.statement: Edison offers multiple implementations of sequences and collections organised using type classes.

L-effects-bet.statement: Many of the authors were consciously making a long-term bet that principled control of effects would ultimately prove important, against the mainstream default of effects-by-default.

L-effects-convergence.statement: A convergence is underway: the functional community has learnt the value of effects and a way to tame them while mainstream languages adopt declarative constructs, driven especially by parallelism, which punishes unrestricted effects cruelly.

L-empty-type.statement: A sum of zero alternatives, an empty type, might have been useful but was not appreciated at the time.

L-equations-burstall.statement: Writing functional programs as equations with pattern matching traces to Burstall's structural induction and transformation work.

L-executable-mathematics.statement: Because of referential transparency, Haskell programs can be read as executable mathematics, equations over the category of complete partial orders, so in principle the specification becomes the program.

L-existential-types.statement: Existential quantification is expressed by letting a data constructor mention type variables in its arguments that do not appear in its result, at almost no new complexity.

L-explicit-braces.statement: Explicit braces and semicolons can override layout, important for programs that generate Haskell.

L-explicit-effects.statement: Being explicit about effects is extremely useful and may be one of Haskell's main impacts on mainstream programming.

L-ffi-adhoc.statement: Once the IO monad existed, implementation-specific foreign-call mechanisms appeared quickly, their trouble being that they were tied to one implementation.

L-ffi-c.statement: An implementation-independent Foreign Function Interface treats C as a lowest common denominator, since calling C lets you call almost anything else.

L-ffi-need.statement: A very common application need is to call procedures written in another language from Haskell, and preferably the reverse.

L-ffi-process.statement: The FFI process was open to all but depended critically on one person willing to drive it as Editor, differing in kind from the original language development.

L-ffi-tools.statement: Pre-processing tools (Green Card, H/Direct, C2Hs) emerged to ease writing the many foreign import declarations a large binding requires.

L-first-class-infix.statement: The wish that all values be first class clashed with infix operators not being first class.

L-fix-leaks.statement: Space leaks can be fixed by shortening object lifetimes, not only by adding strictness; sometimes more laziness wins.

L-flat-namespace.statement: As use grew, the completely flat module name space became irksome, since two libraries could not both use the name Map.

L-fp-compilers-productivity.statement: The abstraction and non-interference of functional languages make compilers and translation natural applications with high productivity and little project management.

L-fran-behaviour.statement: Fran's key idea is a behaviour, a first-class time-varying value, really a function from time to values.

L-fran-events.statement: Fran's second idea is a stream of events, with switching combinators connecting continuous behaviours and discrete events for hybrid systems.

L-fran-numeric.statement: Haskell's Num and Floating classes let one add two behaviours or take the sine of a behaviour.

L-functional-dependencies.statement: Functional dependencies declare an explicit dependency between a class's parameters so that fixing some fixes others; informally described yet widely implemented and extremely tricky in detail.

L-gadts.statement: Generalised algebraic data types let a constructor's return type be specified directly, so pattern matching yields type as well as value information.

L-generic-programming.statement: A generic function behaves uniformly over any data type with a few type-specific cases, and Haskell hosted many generic-programming experiments.

L-gf-app.statement: Haskell was chosen for GF, particularly for the compilation and partial-evaluation aspects of grammars, using monads and type classes heavily.

L-ghc-complexity.statement: Over fifteen years GHC grew a huge number of features, making it a dauntingly complex beast to understand and modify.

L-ghc-extensions-early.statement: GHC's first full release already supported extensions beyond Haskell: monadic I/O, mutable arrays, unboxed data types, and space/time profiling.

L-ghc-frontend-fullsyntax.statement: GHC keeps a large front-end data type reflecting Haskell's full syntax so error messages match what the programmer wrote.

L-ghc-in-haskell.statement: GHC proper, begun autumn 1989, was designed as a complete implementation of Haskell in Haskell, bootstrapped via the prototype, sharing only the parser.

L-ghc-origin.statement: GHC began in January 1989 at Glasgow; its first version, written in LML by Kevin Hammond, was essentially a new front end to the Chalmers LML compiler.

L-gmachine.statement: The G-machine showed lazy functional programs could be compiled to efficient code.

L-goals-not-met.statement: Several initial goals were not met: the OL basis, embodying only well-tried ideas, and a formal semantics.

L-gofer-firsts.statement: Gofer was first to implement several type-class features (constructor classes, do-notation, dictionary-free and multi-parameter classes), some later adopted in Haskell 98.

L-gofer-small-interpreter.statement: Gofer was a small C interpreter Jones built to learn, fitting on a single floppy.

L-gofer-to-hugs.statement: Jones rewrote Gofer to track the Haskell standard, renaming it Hugs, whose first release ignored the module system.

L-graph-reduction.statement: Lazy languages were implemented by graph reduction, notably Turner's elegant SK combinators.

L-guards-left.statement: Haskell moved guards to the left of the definition, next to the patterns and suggestive of evaluation order.

L-gui-bindings-ffi.statement: Pragmatist GUI bindings were hampered by the absence of a well-defined foreign-function interface.

L-gui-idealists-pragmatists.statement: Haskell GUI work split into idealists seeking a purely declarative interaction and pragmatists binding to existing toolkits, and none of the declarative GUIs became the toolkit of choice.

L-gui-no-standard.statement: The absence of a single standard Haskell GUI inhibits development, yet no approach has won enough support.

L-haggis-concurrent.statement: Haggis replaced the event loop with lightweight concurrency, and its requirements drove Concurrent Haskell.

L-hardware-fp.statement: Lazy functional languages suit synchronous hardware: lazy streams model time-varying signals and higher-order functions express circuit structure.

L-haskell-big-implementations.statement: Haskell is a big language and much work to implement, yet several implementations exist, including new ones once thought unlikely.

L-haskell-overcame-impractical.statement: Haskell helped overcome that impracticality by sticking remorselessly to purity and by building a critical mass of interest and research around a single language.

L-haskell-pretty.statement: A pleasing consequence of the syntax effort is that Haskell programs look nice.

L-haskell98-stability.statement: The Haskell 98 Report was a deliberate commitment to stability.

L-haskore.statement: Haskore expresses music declaratively, combining notes and rests with sequential and parallel combinators, enabled by purity, laziness and higher-order functions.

L-hat-project.statement: Hat generalised a trace to support several kinds of debugging as a source-to-source tool, but has not become a regular part of programming.

L-haxml.statement: HaXml offers a flexible single-type combinator library and a more precise but less flexible data-binding approach.

L-hbc-doomed.statement: Being written in LML, hbc was more or less doomed to dwindle though it lived as a test bed for years.

L-hbc-origin.statement: Augustsson and Truvé wrote their own Haskell compiler based on LML rather than wait for the Glasgow compiler.

L-hbc-stumbling.statement: hbc's hard parts were the module system and especially type checking, done before good papers on it existed.

L-heap-profiler.statement: Runciman and Wakeling built a heap profiler classifying heap contents by allocating function or constructor, enabling dramatic space improvements against space leaks.

L-helium.statement: The Helium compiler focuses on teaching and high-quality type error messages.

L-hierarchical-modules.statement: An effort led by Malcolm Wallace specified hierarchical multi-component module names like Data.Map, borrowing largely from Java, swiftly implemented and surviving unchanged.

L-high-level-succinct.statement: As a very high-level language Haskell lets programmers write succinct but readable code and concentrate on the problem without boilerplate and housekeeping.

L-higher-kind-unification.statement: Treating higher-kinded constructors as uninterpreted functions and disallowing type-level lambda lets ordinary first-order unification suffice, an ad hoc solution with excellent power-to-weight ratio.

L-higher-kinds.statement: Type classes were generalised to higher kinds, giving constructor classes.

L-higher-rank-types.statement: Higher-rank types allow abstracting over a polymorphic function; inference needs a few explicit annotations, first implemented in GHC in 2000.

L-hood.statement: HOOD is a lightweight debugger where inserted observe calls collect and print values by tag, showing how much of a lazy input was needed.

L-house-os.statement: House implemented a whole operating system in Haskell, using a monad for IA32 access including virtual memory and low-level IO.

L-hugs-merged.statement: The parallel Yale and Nottingham Hugs versions were confusing and were merged in Hugs 98, the first to support Haskell 98.

L-hugs-slowed.statement: Hugs development slowed after Hugs 98, benefiting from Haskell 98's stability while still adding features.

L-hugs-typechecker.statement: Jones overhauled the Hugs type checker with experimental support for advanced type-system features.

L-hunit.statement: HUnit supports traditional unit testing, providing ways to define, structure and run test cases automatically.

L-imperative-fp-name.statement: Peyton Jones and Wadler named the world-passing token implementation of IO "imperative functional programming".

L-implicit-parameters.statement: Implicit parameters, a further instance of qualified types, make parameter passing happen implicitly like dictionary passing, understood as selective dynamic scoping.

L-industrial-haskell.statement: So many extensions have appeared since Haskell 98 that few real programs adhere to the standard, a problem for users, tool builders and teachers that motivates a new Industrial Haskell standard.

L-infix-binds-less.statement: Infix application always binds less tightly than function application, so f x + g y needs no parentheses.

L-infix-from-day-one.statement: Wanting expressions to look like mathematics, the committee adopted infix operators from day one.

L-influence-csharp.statement: Features of C# were pioneered by Haskell and other functional languages, with LINQ inspired by monad comprehensions.

L-io-a-computation.statement: The key idea of monadic I/O is to treat a value of type IO a as a computation that, when performed, may do input and output before delivering a value of type a.

L-io-exceptions.statement: The IO monad supports exceptions through ioError and catch, letting programs recover from errors and match failures without giving up deterministic pure semantics.

L-io-implementation.statement: Monadically specified I/O can be implemented with continuations or, in GHC, with a world-passing type where a dummy token ensures sequencing under laziness.

L-io-textbooks.statement: Haskell input/output and the awkward squad are poorly covered by textbooks that present only the purely functional aspects.

L-ioref.statement: From the beginning the IO monad could support mutable locations and arrays via newIORef, readIORef and writeIORef.

L-isabelle-class-laws.statement: In Isabelle, declaring a type class can carry the laws its operations obey and declaring an instance requires proving the instance satisfies them.

L-jhc.statement: jhc uses whole-program analysis for aggressive optimisation, implementing type classes without dictionary-passing.

L-keywords-low.statement: Keeping the number of reserved keywords low was a priority, avoiding ones useful as variable names.

L-kinds-classify.statement: Kinds classify types as types classify values; * is type and *->* a type-level function.

L-lambda-backslash.statement: Anonymous functions use backslash, closest ASCII to lambda, with -> so the period is reserved for composition.

L-lambda-calculus-model.statement: Landin and Strachey established the lambda calculus as fundamental for modelling programming languages.

L-lambda-precedence-change.statement: The committee changed lambda's precedence in infix contexts late in design to avoid piling up parentheses in continuation-style code.

L-lava-classes.statement: Clever use of the class system let Lava use signals-of-lists and lists-of-signals almost interchangeably.

L-lava-sharing.statement: Capturing sharing was tricky since two intended-different fragments are indistinguishable under Haskell's semantics; Lava used a circuit monad.

L-layout-complex-spec.statement: The layout rule grew complex enough to be formally specified, yet most users adopt a conforming style.

L-layout-rule-design.statement: Haskell exploits the physical layout of the text via the offside rule, in a design more lenient than Miranda's.

L-laziness-combinators.statement: Laziness makes Haskell natural for combinator libraries, allowing recursive combinators without fuss and unusual control flow.

L-laziness-lifetimes.statement: By abstracting from evaluation order laziness also abstracts from object lifetimes, which is why it contributes to space leaks.

L-laziness-macros.statement: Lazy evaluation gives much of the power of Lisp macros through ordinary function definitions.

L-lazy-appeal.statement: Lazy evaluation appealed through its link to call-by-name lambda calculus, infinite data structures, and simple implementation.

L-lazy-enables-stream.statement: Lazy evaluation lets a program generate a request before processing any responses, which makes the stream I/O model work.

L-lazy-three-times.statement: Lazy evaluation was invented independently three times, igniting interest in lazy functional languages.

L-lazy-unpredictable.statement: Lazy evaluation's operational aspects are not predictable from the source, making conventional profiling and debugging hard.

L-legacy-influence.statement: Haskell's most important legacy will be its influence on the languages that succeed it, the ideas and techniques it nurtured proving of enduring value even after Haskell itself is forgotten.

L-let-and-where.statement: The assumption of one way to do something was abandoned; both let and where are fully supported.

L-letwhere-lazy-wart.statement: Pattern matching in let and where is always lazy, unlike case and lambda, a wart in the design.

L-libraries-modest-evolution.statement: The standard libraries are modest while real applications need richer ones, driving an informal library evolution mechanism.

L-library-report.statement: Haskell 1.3 added a Library Report, since programs can hardly be portable without standard libraries.

L-lifetime-profiling.statement: Extending the profiler to object lifetimes revealed data not yet needed (lag), never used again (drag), or never used (void).

L-lifted-tuples.statement: Tuples and algebraic data types were made lifted so matching always evaluates, with lazy matching reintroduced via tilde-patterns.

L-linspire-uniformity.statement: Haskell has versatility comparable to shell and scripting languages but promotes much greater uniformity, though its idioms for systems programming are not quite as compact as Perl's.

L-listcomp-lazy-popular.statement: List comprehensions are more popular in lazy languages, found in Miranda and Haskell but not SML or Scheme.

L-listcomp-monads-reverted.statement: Haskell 1.4 generalised list comprehensions to arbitrary monads, reversed in Haskell 98.

L-listcomp-notation.statement: List comprehensions give convenient notation for maps, filters and Cartesian products, from Darlington, Turner and named by Wadler.

L-literate-comments.statement: Haskell added literate comments reversing the usual convention, marking code lines with a special mark.

L-lolita.statement: In LOLITA laziness was essential to handle the explosion of syntactic and semantic ambiguity from a large grammar.

L-loops-recursion-hard.statement: Simple loop programs can be harder for students to grasp when expressed using recursion.

L-many-ways-fit.statement: Haskell offers many ways to define functions, simple and fitting together sensibly.

L-matching-semantics.statement: Haskell chose top-to-bottom equation matching over order-independent alternatives like tightest match, sequential equations and uniform patterns.

L-math-look-teaching.statement: Haskell's mathematical look and feel makes it a medium for teaching discrete mathematics and logic.

L-minimal-surfaces.statement: Haskell's language, libraries and culture lead to solutions that feel like minimal surfaces: simple expressions comprising significant complexity, with natural forms recurring problem after problem.

L-minimalist-records.statement: Haskell 1.3 adopted Mark Jones's minimalist record syntax as sugar over algebraic data types, leaving the field open for richer proposals.

L-miranda-identified-bottom.statement: Miranda identified bottom with (bottom, bottom), making currying an exact isomorphism, which influenced the committee.

L-miranda-mature.statement: Miranda was the most mature lazy language, the natural starting-point candidate.

L-miranda-typing.statement: Miranda added strong polymorphic typing and type inference, proven in ML, to the untyped SASL and KRC.

L-module-interfaces.statement: Early Haskell required module interfaces as well as implementations, surfacing issues of duplication and tension; interfaces were abandoned in Haskell 1.4, leaving the language regrettably without a formally checked interface language.

L-module-little-debate.statement: Haskell's module system emerged with surprisingly little debate; the anticipated argument over adopting ML's module system never happened, perhaps for lack of an advocate or tacit agreement it was a bridge too far with type classes.

L-module-namespace-only.statement: They converged on a simple design where the module system is only a namespace-control mechanism, specified separately from the type system.

L-module-not-distribution.statement: Modules are a unit of program construction but not of distribution; developers want to ship a group of modules as a package, which the language did not address.

L-moggi-monads.statement: Moggi used monads from category theory to modularise denotational semantics, systematising features such as state and exceptions.

L-monad-as-typeclass.statement: A monad is a programming pattern expressible directly in Haskell as a type class, giving practical use for combinators that work for any monad.

L-monad-definition.statement: A monad is a type constructor M with return and bind, where M a is a computation returning a value of type a and bind sequences such computations.

L-monad-laws.statement: A true monad's return and bind must satisfy three laws of associative composition with identity, which Haskell provides no mechanism to enforce.

L-monad-transformers.statement: Monad transformers abstract over combining monads, but monads do not compose modularly, an open research problem.

L-monadic-advantage.statement: The big advantage of monadic I/O is conceptual: thinking in terms of computations is easier than in terms of continuations, and the abstraction hides changeable details.

L-monadic-dominated.statement: The monadic approach dominated earlier I/O models because its types are more compact, informative and polymorphic.

L-monadic-io.statement: Haskell 1.3 introduced monadic I/O with do syntax, dropping the earlier I/O semantics.

L-monads-io-area.statement: Monads and input/output are a distinctive area of the language's evolution.

L-monads-side-effects-examples.statement: Many notions of side effect are definable as monads: state transformer, state reader, exception, continuation, list, and parser.

L-monomorphism-restriction.statement: The monomorphism restriction forces a definition that does not look like a function to be monomorphic in overloaded variables, adopted to avoid silently duplicating computation but judged a wart.

L-multiparam-resisted.statement: Type classes can be generalised from a predicate over one type to a relation over several, but the committee resisted multi-parameter classes as an unforced step into ambiguity and kept the single-parameter restriction.

L-namespaces.statement: Namespaces were defined orthogonal when needed and overlapping when context sufficed, so one capitalised name can mean several things.

L-naming-moment.statement: The moment a language is named is a small but important moment in its evolution.

L-naturals-unary.statement: A type isomorphic to the naturals allows pattern matching but its unary representation is inefficient.

L-need-common-language.statement: The lack of a common language held back functional programming, motivating a single language all the groups could share.

L-newtype.statement: newtype introduces a type isomorphic to an existing one, an unlifted single-constructor type motivated by abstract data types.

L-nhc-space-motivation.statement: Röjemo built nhc to be space-efficient and bootstrap in much smaller memory than hbc or GHC.

L-nhc-york-profiling.statement: nhc's development used York heap-profiling tools, bringing Röjemo to York and more space-efficient methods.

L-nk-brackets.statement: With n+k, apparently redundant brackets change meaning: n + 1 = 7 defines +, (n + 1) = 7 defines n.

L-nk-controversy.statement: n+k patterns were controversial and nearly removed, but stayed in the language.

L-nk-efficiency.statement: n+k patterns give pattern matching's benefits without loss of efficiency, a special case of a view.

L-nk-wadler-history.statement: n+k patterns were suggested by Wadler, first seen in Gödel's proof, earlier in NPL and Miranda.

L-non-strict-pure.statement: The language to be designed was fixed as non-strict and purely functional.

L-non-von-neumann.statement: The hope that laziness would lead to non-von Neumann hardware proved largely a dead end.

L-not-from-miranda.statement: Not starting from Miranda forced a new design but allowed more radical approaches such as type classes.

L-numeric-classes.statement: The collection of numeric type classes reflects an uneasy compromise between algebraic purity (more classes) and pragmatism (fewer).

L-numeric-kinds.statement: Haskell's type system was extended in Bluespec with types of numeric kind so the class system can do statically checked arithmetic, giving accurate types to bit vectors.

L-observable-sharing.statement: Claessen used unsafePerformIO for observable sharing, which has a tractable theory despite its unsafe implementation.

L-ol-default.statement: OL's design was the default to be kept for any topic lacking a clearly better solution.

L-one-prefix-operator.statement: Haskell has only one prefix operator, negation; the committee wanted none but would not force minus 42.

L-open-participation.statement: After the committee ceased, anyone on the mailing list could participate, with Peyton Jones as editor.

L-overloaded-literals.statement: Overloaded numeric literals gave fib the type Num a => a -> a, raising pattern matching's complexity.

L-paper-is-history.statement: The paper is meant as a history rather than a technical description or tutorial.

L-parametricity-debate.statement: Launchbury held parametricity too important to give up while Hughes wanted seq applicable to any type, two virtually incompatible goals.

L-parametricity-deforestation.statement: Parametricity justifies short-cut deforestation (the foldr/build rule), which needs a rank-2 type for build.

L-parser-bnf.statement: Parser combinators allow an extraordinarily direct transcription of BNF into executable code.

L-parser-history.statement: Parser combinators go back to Burge and were brought to wider attention by Wadler's list-of-successes paper.

L-parser-monad.statement: Wanting a parser to return a value dovetails with the monad, giving a parameterised Parser and do-notation.

L-parser-new-combinators.statement: Programmers can easily build new parser combinators from existing ones.

L-parser-type.statement: A parser can be modelled as a function from a string to a list of depleted input strings, failure being the empty list.

L-pattern-match-lazy-complex.statement: Pattern matching semantics is more complex in lazy languages, since match order can change termination.

L-pattern-readability.statement: Pattern matching against algebraic data types greatly increases readability.

L-ph.statement: pH adopted Haskell's syntax and type system but kept Id's eager, parallel evaluation, I-structures and M-structures.

L-polymorphic-recursion.statement: Polymorphic recursion lets a function be used polymorphically in its own definition; hard to infer but easy to check, so allowed only with an explicit signature.

L-postmortem-debugging.statement: Post-mortem debugging waits until execution completes so needed values are known, abstracting from evaluation order.

L-practical-areas.statement: As Haskell found real use, attention turned to practically important areas the original designers had neglected, still recent and in flux.

L-pretty-doc.statement: A pretty-printing document is an abstract type conceptually a function from available width to a layout, though it need not be implemented as one.

L-profiler-faster.statement: The profiler quickly led to faster Haskell programs, speeding up GHC itself twofold.

L-programming-environment.statement: Until recently, Yale Haskell excepted, implementers paid little attention to the programming environment, though that is beginning to change.

L-programming-large.statement: Support for programming in the large (modules, packages, foreign-function interface) is a technical area of Haskell.

L-prototype-haskell10.statement: The prototype compiler implemented essentially all of Haskell 1.0 including views, type classes, deriving, the module system, binary I/O, streams and continuations.

L-public-lists.statement: Discomfort with public and private mailing lists moved debate fully public, though the committee still decided.

L-pure-not-right-way.statement: Purely functional programming is not necessarily the right way to write programs.

L-pure-principled-attack.statement: Functional programming, particularly in its purely functional form, is a radical and principled attack on the challenge of writing programs that work.

L-purity-io-problem.statement: The committee's firm commitment to a pure language made the design of the I/O system a central problem, fearing a weak solution would make Haskell look like a toy.

L-qualified-types.statement: Type classes are one instance of Jones's more general framework of qualified types, which also yields polymorphic extensible records with lacks predicates witnessed at run time.

L-quickcheck.statement: QuickCheck tests programs against specifications written as boolean functions invoked on random data, displaying counter-examples on failure.

L-quickcheck-emulated.statement: QuickCheck's design has been emulated in other languages, finding real bugs.

L-quickcheck-exemplifies.statement: QuickCheck exemplifies Haskell's features: a DSL of testable properties, the class system, and monadic generators.

L-quickcheck-programmers.statement: QuickCheck succeeded partly because Haskell programmers prefer writing formal specifications to writing test code.

L-quirky-elegance.statement: What first drew many of the authors to the field was the quirky elegance of the purely functional approach.

L-random-seed.statement: The Haskell 98 Random library uses the IO monad as a source of seeds.

L-realworld-impact.statement: Real-world impact was an important goal of the Committee; Haskell is not mainstream but fares well in niches owing to specific language characteristics.

L-records-omitted.statement: Records with named fields were omitted from early Haskell because there was no obvious right design.

L-redex-trails.statement: Redex trails let programmers step backwards through execution.

L-report-book-online.statement: Publishing the Report as a book while keeping it free online defused a debate about freedom and intellectual property.

L-retainer-profiling.statement: Retainer profiling explains why data was not garbage-collected by showing which objects point at it.

L-runst.statement: Imperative computations can be securely encapsulated in a pure function via a state monad parameterised by a type s, encapsulated by runST with a rank-2 type and parametricity preventing reference leaks.

L-sasl-higher-order.statement: Turner's SASL was a pure higher-order functional language, a sugared lambda calculus with lexical scoping and pattern matching.

L-sasl-os.statement: SASL was used at Burroughs to build an entire operating system, likely the first large-scale pure lazy functional programming.

L-scheme-cbv.statement: Scheme stayed call-by-value because simulating call-by-name via thunks is easier than the reverse.

L-scoped-type-variables.statement: Lexically scoped type variables are required to write signatures for inner functions; their omission from Haskell 98 was in retrospect a mistake since polymorphic recursion and higher-rank types need signatures.

L-section-negation.statement: Sections introduced an ambiguity around negation, seen as a problem with prefix operators rather than sections.

L-sections.statement: A section is a partial application of an infix operator, parenthesised into a first-class value.

L-segregate-formats.statement: Explicitly segregating legacy data formats into separate data types prevented the mysterious errors that propagate through shell programs when a format changes.

L-seq-controversial.statement: seq was controversial for its effect on semantics, not definable in the lambda calculus and the only way to distinguish a divergent function from bottom.

L-seq-eval-class.statement: Haskell 1.3 made seq overloaded via a class Eval recording its uses so parametricity restrictions were visible, later removed in Haskell 98.

L-seq-for-speed.statement: seq was introduced primarily to improve speed by helping the strictness analyser, not to fix space leaks.

L-seq-introduced.statement: Haskell 1.3 introduced seq and strictness annotations to give the programmer control over evaluation order.

L-seq-miranda.statement: seq and strict data components were already present in Miranda for the same reasons.

L-seq-parametricity.statement: seq does not satisfy the parametricity property for its type and so weakens the parametricity and free theorems of functions that use it.

L-seq-polymorphic-today.statement: seq today is a simple polymorphic function, sacrificing parametricity for agility and leaving GHC's short-cut deforestation unsound.

L-seq-space-debugging.statement: Hughes wanted Haskell's seq to support space debugging well.

L-shadowing-allowed.statement: Haskell allowed variable shadowing, since outlawing it is inconsistent with alpha renaming.

L-single-constructor-tuple.statement: Whether single-constructor data types share tuple properties raises a semantic discontinuity when a second constructor is added.

L-space-sensitivity.statement: Haskell's space use is extremely sensitive to evaluation order, hard to anticipate but fixable by tiny changes with good profiling.

L-start-from-existing.statement: The easiest way forward was to begin with an existing language and evolve it.

L-state-monad-plumbing.statement: Lacking reference cells, threading a counter by hand to generate fresh names is tedious and error-prone; a state transformer monad hides the plumbing.

L-stm.statement: MVars make programs non-composable, and software transactional memory is a promising approach to that composition problem that fits Haskell particularly well.

L-stream-cont-equivalent.statement: Stream and continuation I/O turned out to be functionally equivalent, each expressible in terms of the other.

L-stream-model.statement: In the stream model a program is a value of type Behaviour mapping responses to requests, needing no special I/O syntax and defined by how the OS interprets it.

L-stream-primitive-efficiency.statement: Defining streams from continuations was inefficient (linear space, quadratic time), so Haskell 1.0 took streams as primitive and defined continuations from them though continuations were easier to use.

L-strict-lazy-mix.statement: A main difficulty is constructing software that uses both strict and lazy evaluation well.

L-sum-of-products.statement: Haskell took from Miranda defining algebraic types as a sum of products, unlike Hope and SML which separated sums and products.

L-syntax-effort.statement: The committee worked hard on syntax, which as the user interface is personal and provoked heated debate.

L-syntax-io-retrospect.statement: In retrospect the authors ask whether a syntactic device like do-notation could have made stream or continuation I/O look more natural.

L-teaching-effective.statement: Teaching with Haskell drives fundamental concepts like types and recursion home early and lets students tackle more ambitious problems sooner than in a language like Java.

L-teaching-goal.statement: Suitability for teaching was one of the explicit goals the designers set for Haskell.

L-template-haskell.statement: GHC supports type-safe meta-programming, inspired by C++ template meta-programming and MetaML's staged type system.

L-tools-research.statement: Developing successful profiling and debugging tools for Haskell took considerable research from the early 1990s.

L-top-to-bottom-left-right.statement: Matching is top-to-bottom and left-to-right, important in a lazy language since a non-match passes to the next equation.

L-trace-garbled.statement: Unpredictable evaluation order makes conventional trace printing garble its output.

L-turner-declined.statement: Turner declined to let Miranda be the basis, committed to a single standard while the committee wanted freedom to extend and distribute.

L-turner-lazy-lists.statement: Turner showed the elegance of lazy evaluation and lazy lists emulating many behaviours.

L-two-comment-styles.statement: Haskell had two comment styles, line comments and nestable block comments for commenting out code.

L-two-styles.statement: Two styles emerged: declaration style (equations, pattern matching, guards) and expression style (let, lambda, case, if).

L-type-class-ambiguity.statement: Type classes brought ambiguity: when nothing fixes an intermediate type and the choice matters, the program is rejected pending a signature.

L-type-class-applications.statement: Once adopted, type classes were immediately applied to equality and ordering, string conversion, enumerations, numeric operations and array indexing.

L-type-class-basics.statement: A class declaration specifies methods and their types; a type is made an instance via an instance declaration providing an implementation.

L-type-class-chaos.statement: The world of type classes grew chaotically complex, and despite attempts to bring order a unifying simplifying insight is still awaited.

L-type-class-generalisations.statement: Over time type classes were generalised in varied and surprising ways, some summarised in a 1997 paper on the design space.

L-type-class-origin.statement: Type classes were proposed early by Wadler and Blott as a principled solution to a small problem, overloading for numeric operations and equality.

L-type-class-serendipity.statement: Type classes were serendipitous: invented at the right moment, rapidly pervasive, and opening far richer opportunities than their initial purpose.

L-type-classes-distinctive.statement: The type system, and type classes in particular, are a distinctive contribution of Haskell.

L-type-classes-influence.statement: Type classes were picked up elsewhere: Java 5's bounded generic types and Scala's view bounds and implicit parameters are closely related to them.

L-type-lab.statement: Haskell became an unforeseen laboratory for designing, implementing and applying type-system extensions, for technical reasons (purity, qualified types, abandoned full inference) and nontechnical ones (an innovation-friendly committee, experimenting implementations, a geeky user base).

L-type-level-programming.statement: Multi-parameter classes with functional dependencies allow arbitrary logic-programming-style computation at the type level, at the risk of non-termination in the type checker.

L-type-system-anarchic.statement: Haskell's type system developed anarchically, features used before formalisation, speeding exploration at the cost of complexity.

L-typeclass-compiler-cost.statement: Type classes made the LML-based compiler bigger and slower, and this experience drove the monomorphism restriction and the removal of views.

L-unlifted-indistinguishable.statement: Under unlifted semantics bottom and (bottom, bottom) stay indistinguishable, pattern matching read as binding via fst and snd.

L-unlifted-seq.statement: Unlifted tuples are incompatible with seq, which would require parallel evaluation.

L-unsafeperformio.statement: Unlike runST there is no safe escape from the IO monad, yet all implementations provide unsafePerformIO, whose use is a promise that repetition and ordering do not matter.

L-user-infix-operators.statement: Infix operators are user-definable, including precedence and associativity.

L-views-excluded.statement: Views were in the original design, were removed, and have not been readmitted.

L-views-tension.statement: Wadler suggested views to ease the tension between pattern matching and data abstraction, via an isomorphism.

L-wadler-monads-programs.statement: Wadler recognised that Moggi's semantic technique could structure ordinary functional programs, using monads to express the features Moggi used them to describe.

L-wadlers-law.statement: Wadler's law: effort was spent more on lower-level syntax, most of all on the syntax of comments.

L-web-invert.statement: A web application is better written as a single program calling a primitive that takes an HTML form and returns the responses.

L-web-static-types.statement: The web approach works with a static type system guaranteeing the form's returned type matches what the application expects.

L-where-clause.statement: A where clause attaches to a declaration, scopes over guards and right-hand sides, with lazy bindings.

L-world-passing-rejected.statement: A world-passing model updating world state as data was rejected for lack of an easy way to ensure single-threaded access, later solved by Clean's uniqueness types.

L-yale-environment.statement: The Lisp base let Yale focus on the environment, first to support compiled and interpreted code together with an emacs interface.

L-yale-extensions.statement: Yale Haskell supported many language extensions and served as a test bed for new ideas.

L-yale-haskell.statement: Yale Haskell's Common Lisp back end limited it: lazy code ran 3 to 5 times slower because Lisp's imperative nature prevented Haskell-specific optimisations.

L-yale-scheme-backend.statement: Hudak compiled Haskell into Scheme or T and used a Scheme compiler as a back end rather than a stand-alone compiler.

L-yale-scratchpad.statement: Yale Haskell offered a scratch pad extending a module with definitions without recompiling it.

L-yale-strictness-compilation.statement: Yale Haskell used strictness analysis and type information to compile the strict part of Haskell into efficient Lisp.

L-yampa.statement: Yampa, an arrow-based version of FRP, improved both modularity and performance.
